title: A PROPHET WAS KILLED BY A LION BECAUSE HE DISOBEYED ONE COMMAND FROM GOD
paragraphs:
A PROPHET WAS KILLED BY A LION BECAUSE HE DISOBEYED ONE COMMAND FROM GOD
He survived confronting a king. He resisted money. He walked away obedient. Then one believable lie made him turn back—and what happened next should terrify every Christian who thinks yesterday’s obedience can replace hearing God today.
There was a dead man lying in the road.
Beside him stood a lion.
And beside the lion stood a donkey.
But the lion was not eating the body.
It was not attacking the donkey.
It simply stood there.
Almost like a guard beside the consequences of one terrible decision.
The story is found in 1 Kings 13, and Scripture never even gives us the dead man’s name. It repeatedly calls him אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִים — ’ish ha’Elohim — “the man of God.”
That is what makes this story so unsettling.
This was not presented as the downfall of some openly pagan rebel who hated God.
This was a man God had used.
A man entrusted with a word from the LORD.
A man courageous enough to stand before a king.
A man through whom God had already demonstrated supernatural power.
And yet before the day was over, his body would be lying beneath the open sky because he abandoned a command God had personally given him.
If you have ever thought, “God has used me, so I must be okay,” keep reading.
If you have ever confused spiritual experience with spiritual safety, keep reading.
If you have ever allowed another person’s voice to overrule something Scripture had already made clear, keep reading.
Because the lion is not the most frightening thing in this story.
The most frightening thing is how believable the deception sounded.

Israel was spiritually fractured. Jeroboam had become king over the northern tribes and, fearing that continued worship in Jerusalem might eventually turn the people’s loyalty back toward the house of David, established alternative centers of worship.
Golden calves appeared.
An altar stood at Bethel.
Political convenience began dressing itself in religious clothing.
Then God sent an unnamed man of God from Judah to Bethel.
Imagine the scene.
King Jeroboam is standing beside the altar.
Incense is being burned.
The religious machinery of the kingdom is functioning.
Then an outsider walks into the middle of it carrying a word nobody in power wants to hear.
He cries against the altar by the word of the LORD and announces that a future descendant of David named Josiah will desecrate it.
Then he gives a sign.
The altar will split apart.
Its ashes will spill out.
Jeroboam does not repent.
He reaches out his hand and orders:
“Seize him!”
Then the king’s hand dries up.
He cannot pull it back.
And the altar splits.
The ashes pour out.
Suddenly the man whom the king wanted arrested is the man the king needs.
Jeroboam asks him to plead with God for the restoration of his hand.
The man of God does.
God restores it.
Think about how spiritually dangerous this moment could have become.
The man has confronted political power and survived.
A miracle has confirmed his message.
A king has experienced judgment and healing in front of him.
Now Jeroboam offers hospitality and a reward.
But the man of God refuses.
He explains why.
“For so was it charged me by the word of the LORD, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest.”
—1 Kings 13:9, KJV
The Hebrew expression behind “word of the LORD” is דְּבַר־יְהוָה — devar-YHWH.
This was not a preference.
Not intuition.
Not merely a feeling.
God had spoken.
Do not eat there.
Do not drink there.
Do not return by the same road.
And initially, the man obeyed.
He refused the king’s table.
He refused the king’s reward.
He walked away.
If the story ended there, we would remember him as an extraordinary example of courage and obedience.
But it did not end there.
Because sometimes the temptation that cannot make you fall while you are standing before an enemy will return wearing the face of someone who sounds spiritual.
An old prophet living in Bethel heard what had happened.
His sons told him about the man of God.
The old prophet saddled a donkey, pursued him and eventually found him sitting beneath an oak.
“Art thou the man of God that camest from Judah?”
“I am.”
Then came the invitation.
“Come home with me, and eat bread.”
The man of God gave the correct answer.
He repeated God's command.
He knew what God had told him.
Then the old prophet said something devastating:
“I am a prophet also as thou art.”
And then he claimed that an angel had spoken to him “by the word of the LORD,” instructing him to bring the man of God home so he could eat and drink.
Then Scripture gives us five chilling words in the King James Version:
“But he lied unto him.”
—1 Kings 13:18
Read that again.
He lied.
The invitation sounded spiritual.
The messenger had religious credentials.
An angel was invoked.
God's name was attached to the claim.
Hospitality seemed harmless.
But it contradicted what God had already said.
And the man of God went back.
That is where this ancient story suddenly walks into our lives.
Because deception does not always arrive looking evil.
Sometimes it carries a Bible.
Sometimes it knows Christian vocabulary.
Sometimes it says, “God told me.”
Sometimes it comes from someone older.
Someone respected.
Someone experienced.
Someone with a ministry.
Someone who sounds more confident about God's will for your life than you are.
But no human being receives authority to make God's revealed truth false.
The New Testament later gives Christians an indispensable principle:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.”
—1 John 4:1, KJV
The Greek verb translated “try” or “test” is δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete.
Test.
Examine.
Discern.
Do not surrender discernment merely because somebody uses spiritual language.
Paul goes even further in Galatians 1:8. Even if “an angel from heaven” preached a gospel contrary to the apostolic Gospel, believers were not to receive it.
That does not mean 1 Kings 13 and Galatians 1 are describing identical situations. They are not.
But the principle should sober us.
A supernatural claim does not outrank God's truth.
A charismatic personality does not outrank God's truth.
A title does not outrank God's truth.
A viral preacher does not outrank God's truth.
A dream does not outrank God's truth.
A feeling does not outrank God's truth.
And neither does Gospel Warrior.
Test what you read here against Scripture.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
His Word does not need our manipulation to remain true.
The tragedy in 1 Kings 13 is that the man of God already knew what God had commanded.
His problem was not lack of revelation.
His problem was abandoning the revelation he had received because another voice offered a contradiction wrapped in spiritual credibility.
So he went back.
He sat at the table.
He ate bread.
He drank water.
And then something extraordinary happened.
The same old prophet who had lied to bring him back suddenly received a genuine word from the LORD.
Imagine the silence at that table.
The meal is still there.
The man of God has already crossed the boundary.
Then judgment is announced.
“Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth of the LORD, and hast not kept the commandment which the LORD thy God commanded thee…”
—1 Kings 13:21, KJV
The Hebrew narrative uses the language of rebelling against the “mouth” of the LORD—פִּי יְהוָה, pi YHWH.
That image is painfully personal.
God had spoken.
The man had heard.
The man had obeyed…
until he did not.
After eating and drinking, he leaves.
Then the lion finds him.
Scripture says:
“And when he was gone, a lion met him by the way, and slew him: and his carcase was cast in the way, and the ass stood by it, the lion also stood by the carcase.”
—1 Kings 13:24, KJV
The scene is deliberately strange.
Normally a lion that kills prey eats.
Normally a donkey standing beside a lion does not calmly remain there.
Yet the text emphasizes the lion, the donkey and the body standing together.

Later, when the old prophet hears about it, he says that this was the man of God who had disobeyed the word of the LORD, and that the LORD had delivered him to the lion according to the word spoken to him.
We should be careful here.
This passage does not teach that every tragedy is God's punishment for a particular act of disobedience.

Jesus Himself rejected simplistic assumptions that suffering automatically identifies someone as a worse sinner than everybody else. Scripture gives us Job. Scripture gives us martyrs. Scripture gives us faithful believers who suffer terribly.
So do not use this passage as a weapon against grieving people.
That would abuse the text.
But we should not soften what this particular text actually says either.
Within the narrative of 1 Kings 13, the man's death is explicitly connected to his disobedience.
And perhaps one of the most uncomfortable details is this:
The liar lived.
The deceived man died.
That bothers us.
It is supposed to bother us.
Why wasn't the old prophet killed?
Why did the man of God bear such severe consequences after being deceived?
The passage does not answer every question our emotions want answered.
And we should not invent explanations God did not give.
But it does destroy one excuse we desperately want to keep:
“Someone else misled me, therefore my obedience no longer matters.”
The old prophet was responsible for lying.
The man of God was responsible for abandoning the command he had received.
Both realities can exist at once.
Someone can genuinely wound you, manipulate you, pressure you or deceive you—and you can still need to bring your own response before God.
That is difficult.
But it is also liberating.
Because repentance begins when we stop handing everyone else ownership of our soul.
Maybe nobody has invited you back to Bethel.
Maybe your “one command” looked different.
You knew that relationship was pulling you away from Christ.
But somebody said, “God wants you happy.”
You knew dishonesty was wrong.
But everybody at work said, “That's just how business is done.”
You knew bitterness was poisoning you.
But someone said, “After what they did, you deserve to hate them.”
You knew sexual sin was destroying your conscience.
But culture renamed conviction “shame” and told you that holiness was repression.
You knew you needed to forgive.
You knew you needed to confess.
You knew you needed to stop pretending.
You knew Scripture said one thing.
But another voice made disobedience sound reasonable.
And somewhere along the road…
you turned back.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because some of us are not reading about an unnamed man from Judah anymore.
We are remembering ourselves.
The moment we compromised.
The secret we protected.
The warning we ignored.
The conviction we kept postponing.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The Bible gathering dust while every other voice became louder.
And perhaps underneath all of it is a terrifying question:
Have I gone too far?
This is where we must be careful not to turn 1 Kings 13 into something it was never meant to be.
The Christian Gospel is not:
“Obey perfectly or God will send a lion after you.”
The Gospel is that none of us has obeyed perfectly.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
—Romans 3:23, KJV
Every one of us has turned aside.
Every one of us needs mercy.
And God did not send Jesus Christ merely to make bad people behave better.
He sent His Son to save sinners.
Jesus obeyed where we failed.
Christ went all the way to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Lion we should ultimately behold is not the lion beside the road in 1 Kings 13.
It is the One Revelation calls “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”
Jesus Christ.
And here is the breathtaking difference.
When our disobedience deserved judgment, Christ stepped into the place of sinners.
Not so that sin could become harmless.
Not so repentance could become optional.
But so guilty people could actually be forgiven, reconciled to God and transformed.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance: a turning, a change of mind that bears itself out in a changed direction.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about where you are.
It is turning toward God.
That means if this article is exposing something you have hidden, your next step is not despair.
It is Jesus.
If you compromised, turn to Jesus.
If you have been spiritually numb, turn to Jesus.
If another person's voice became louder than Scripture, turn to Jesus.
If you have been living two lives, turn to Jesus.
If you have been performing Christianity publicly while starving privately, turn to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
There is grace for sinners who come to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9, KJV
That is why our message is not “From Scandal to Better Behavior.”
It is From Scandal to Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes Peter after denial and makes him a shepherd.
He takes persecuting Saul and makes him Paul, a servant of Christ.
He takes shame and gives forgiveness.
He takes rebellion and calls us to repentance.
He takes dead hearts and gives life.
He does not rewrite the past by pretending the sin never happened.
He rewrites what sin gets to do with the rest of your story.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest spiritual battle happens after everybody thinks you have gone to sleep.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending you are stronger than you are.
Then stop pretending before Jesus.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two honest words are enough to tell another believer, “I need somebody standing with me.”
And if Christ has already brought you through a season of compromise, deception, addiction, bitterness, shame or spiritual wandering, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Not because saving a Facebook post makes anyone spiritual, but because there are warnings we need to read twice.
Send it to the believer who has been hearing too many voices and opening Scripture too little.
But do it with love.
Not accusation.
“Lord, keep all of us faithful.”
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you return to Scripture, think more deeply about Christ, repent more honestly, or keep fighting when your faith felt exhausted, follow and stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite the person who does not even believe yet but is willing to listen.

We want this community filled with daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment that ultimately points beyond Gospel Warrior to Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves your faith.
It does not.
Not because anyone can purchase blessing, salvation or spiritual status.
They cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be bought.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
But Christians can freely choose to support ministry work they believe is faithfully serving others.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper with us:
But before you leave this page, remember the unnamed man lying beside the road.
He had courage.
He had gifting.
He had experienced God's power.
He had spoken truth to a king.
And none of yesterday's obedience gave him permission to ignore God's word today.
That may be the warning somebody reading this needs.
Do not build your confidence on the fact that God used you yesterday.
Stay close to Christ today.
Do not assume every spiritual-sounding voice came from God.
Test it.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Listen.
Obey.
And when you fail—and every Christian still desperately needs grace—do not run away from the Savior because you are ashamed of needing a Savior.
Run toward Him.
The road back to Jesus is called repentance.
And the arms waiting there are scarred by the price He paid to redeem sinners.
The man of God turned back toward Bethel and found judgment on the road.
But if you have wandered from God, you are being called in another direction today.
Back to Christ.
Back to truth.
Back to repentance.
Back to grace.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or simply:
“No more hiding.”
Because perhaps the most dangerous turn in your life will not look like rebellion when you make it.
It may look reasonable.
It may sound spiritual.
It may even come from someone you trust.
But when every other voice has finished speaking, there is still only one King worthy of your life.
Jesus Christ.
And if you remember only one sentence after you close this article, remember this:
The voice that persuaded you to turn away from God does not get the final word over the life that turns back to Jesus.
